title: Coupons at checkout: what one 'use' really counts
head: feature/coupons

steps.title: Two commits, one new endpoint, one changed charge line

blocks.quote:
Apply coupon discounts at checkout and add a coupon API
POST /orders/:id/coupon takes a coupon code and attaches a discount to the order. Checkout charges the total minus the discount.

blocks.p: Both commits were co-written by an AI model. The code will look tidy and typical. So we will not stop at "looks right". We will push concrete values through it.

steps.title: Say the purpose before reading lines

blocks.p: Before opening any file, a senior puts the goal into words. Here it is: the shop can hand out a code worth a fixed yen amount. Each code has a use limit and an expiry date. A customer attaches it to a cart, and checkout charges less.
Who stops having a problem? Marketing can run a campaign like "the first 100 customers get 500 yen off". Customers pay less without anyone touching the database by hand.
Our hypothesis to check in later chapters: if `max_uses` is 100, then 100 customers get the discount. Marketing will read the number that way. We will test whether the code keeps that promise.
In one sentence: the change lets a stored code lower the amount charged at checkout, within a count limit and a date limit.

steps.title: The flow, including what did not change

blocks.pre:
POST /orders/:id/coupon                       (new)
  server.ts readJson -> handleApplyCoupon
    CouponService.apply
      orders.get        status CART or PAYMENT_FAILED?
      coupons.get       exists? not expired?
      coupons.consumeUse   UPDATE used_count + 1
      discount = min(coupon discount, order total)
      orders.save

POST /orders/:id/checkout                (flow unchanged)
  OrderService.checkout
    save PENDING_PAYMENT
    charge(total - discount, key = order-<id>)   <- changed
    -> PAID / PAYMENT_FAILED / stays PENDING

every 5 min: reconcilePendingPayments    (unchanged)
    findCharge(order-<id>) -> PAID or PAYMENT_FAILED

blocks.p: Two unchanged pieces matter here. First, the payment key is built only from the order ID. Second, the reconcile batch looks charges up by that same key. So any change to what we charge also passes through code that this diff did not touch.
The diff is about 300 lines. The thinking happens in about 25 of them: the body of `apply`, the `consumeUse` UPDATE, and the one changed charge line. Everything else follows from adding a field.

blocks.p: We also carry one promise from the old code. Checkout's comment says how a double-clicked button is handled. Keep it in mind.
In one sentence: coupons add a new write path to the order. Checkout then reads one new field from the order, under a payment key that did not change.

steps.title: The use counter: check and add in one statement

blocks.p: The limit check and the increment are one UPDATE. `WHERE used_count < max_uses` makes the database refuse the 101st use. Then `changes` is 0 and `apply` throws `CouponUsedUpError`. With `max_uses = 100` and `used_count = 99`, two requests cannot both pass. Only one row update can win.
The naive version would SELECT the coupon, compare in TypeScript, then UPDATE. In the gap between those steps, a second request could read the same 99. This code avoids that gap.
`orders.coupon_code REFERENCES coupons (code)` really is enforced. A declared foreign key does nothing in SQLite unless the connection turns it on. Here `db.ts` turns it on for every connection.
The idea has a name: avoid check-then-write. Let one conditional write do both jobs.

steps.title: Old orders keep their old price

blocks.p: `discount_amount INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0` gives every existing order a 0 discount. For those orders, checkout charges `total - 0`, the same as before. The migration runs inside BEGIN/COMMIT (`db.ts:17-25`), so it cannot be half applied.

`discountAmount` is required, not optional. That is why every test that builds an `Order` changed. The compiler found each place for the author. All 6 test edits only add `discountAmount: 0` and change no expected value.

steps.title: The line that moves money, and the test that guards it

blocks.p: Remove `- order.discountAmount` and this test fails: it gets 3000, not 2500. So the most important line is pinned by a test. The test goes through `checkout`, the same entry point a user hits.
The coupon tests use a real in-memory SQLite, not a mock. So the UPDATE in `consumeUse` really runs in the use-limit test.
In one sentence: the mechanism promises that a coupon's total uses never exceed `max_uses`, that unchanged orders pay the same, and that checkout charges total minus the stored discount.

Coupon `WELCOME` gives 500 yen off, with `max_uses = 100` and `used_count = 0`. A customer's order `o1` is in CART. They double-click Apply, so two `POST /orders/o1/coupon {"code":"WELCOME"}` requests arrive.

The comment on `consumeUse` says concurrent uses cannot exceed the limit. After both requests finish, what is `used_count`? How much discount does `o1` have? Is the hypothesis from chapter 2 still true?

steps.title: Answer: two uses for one discount

blocks.p: `apply` never looks at `order.couponCode`. Each call that passes the status and expiry checks consumes a use. The second click leaves the order exactly as it was, but burns a second use.

The comment is true, but it promises something smaller than it sounds. It protects the coupon's limit. It says nothing about one use per order. The name `consumeUse` is accurate. The bug is in what `apply` does around it.

The same gap shows up in other ways. If a customer applies A and then B, A's use is never given back. And nothing authenticates this route, the same as checkout in `main`. So anyone with an order ID can POST 100 times and use up a campaign for every other customer.
The tests miss it. The use-limit test (`test/couponService.test.ts:46-51`) applies the coupon to `o1` and `o2`, two different orders. No test applies the coupon twice to the same order.

Weight: **must fix**. It counts against a money budget, and a plain user action triggers it. Checkout already solved double-clicks with a status check. Apply needs its own answer. The general name for this is idempotency: the same request arriving twice must not have a double effect.

steps.title: A fix, and checking that it really prevents the problem

snippet.label: Not in the repository: a possible fix in CouponService.apply, right after the status check

blocks.p: Trace the double-click again. Both repositories use the synchronous `DatabaseSync`. So every `await` inside `apply` resolves without waiting on I/O. Node finishes the first `apply`, including its save, before it starts the second. The second call then sees `couponCode = 'WELCOME'` and returns early. `used_count` stays 1. A followed by B now gets a 409, and A's use is kept for A.

That safety rests on one process and a synchronous driver. If either changes, the read-then-check gap opens again. A guard that holds in any setup would be `UPDATE orders SET coupon_code = ? WHERE id = ? AND coupon_code IS NULL`, run in one transaction with `consumeUse`. It is the same pattern that `consumeUse` already uses.

What the fix does not cover: a cart that applies a coupon and is never checked out still holds a use forever. Should a use count at apply time or at payment? That is a product decision. Ask before merging, and write the answer in a comment.
Add one test: apply `WELCOME` to `o1` twice and assert `usedCount` is 1.

`apply` also accepts orders in PAYMENT_FAILED (`couponService.ts:21`). In `main`, a retry after a decline sends the same key with the same amount. That is tested in `test/orderService.test.ts:37-43`. Now the retry can send the same key `order-o1` with a different amount: 3000 first, then 2500. The cap test also allows a charge of exactly 0 yen (`test/couponService.test.ts:35-39`).

What our code decides: any status other than 402, 429, or 5xx becomes a plain `Error`. Checkout marks PAYMENT_FAILED only for `PaymentDeclinedError`. So if the payment service rejects the request, the order stays PENDING_PAYMENT and the user gets a 500 (`server.ts:27-30`). After 10 minutes, the reconcile batch decides by looking up the same key.

What depends on the payment service is not in this repository. Does it reject a reused key with different parameters? Does it accept amount 0? And what does `findCharge` return for a key whose only charge was declined?

Weight: **question**. Before merging, the author should check the payment service's docs. If the answer is "rejects", the simplest fix is to block coupons on PAYMENT_FAILED orders. Changing the key is harder, because `paymentKeyFor` is shared with the reconcile batch on purpose.

steps.title: Push real values through the expiry check

blocks.p: `expires_at` is `TEXT NOT NULL` with no format check. No code in the repository creates coupons, only the test does. So staff will insert them by hand.
The last row is the dangerous one. A bad value does not fail. It quietly turns the check off. This is JavaScript `Date` behavior, so it is reasoned, not run here.
Weight: **suggestion**. Reject an invalid date in `get()`, or add a format CHECK in the migration. Also write down which time zone the date means.

Finding
Where
rows: Bad JSON body throws in `readJson` and gives 500, not 400. No body size limit.
discount <= total and discount >= 0 are kept only by `apply`; no DB CHECK. Nothing changes `totalAmount` today (grep), so it holds for now.
`CouponService` takes the concrete `SqliteCouponRepository`; orders use the `OrderRepository` interface.
Reused `InvalidOrderStateError` logs "cannot be checked out" on the coupon path.
README still lists only the checkout endpoint.
Expiry is checked at apply, not at checkout. A coupon applied before expiry still discounts after it. Intended?

steps.title: Things that look risky but are fine here

blocks.p: Coupon applied while checkout is charging? Checkout saves PENDING_PAYMENT before it awaits the payment call. `apply` rejects PENDING_PAYMENT. So the coupon cannot slip in after the amount was sent.

`consumeUse` and `orders.save` are not in one transaction. But at that point the save can only fail on a constraint. The coupon code was just read, so the foreign key holds, and the total did not change. A lost use from a failed save is not a realistic path today.
No feature flag? Until staff insert a row into `coupons`, every request returns 404 `coupon_not_found`, and checkout charges `total - 0`. The empty table acts as the switch.
In one sentence: the code keeps the coupon's total under its limit, but it does not promise one use per order. That second promise is the one marketing will assume.

steps.title: Did this change make the codebase better?

blocks.p: Mostly yes. The structure is clean. Old orders are untouched. The counter is safe under concurrency, and the money line is tested. But one must-fix remains: a single order can use up many uses. With that fixed, and the payment question answered, it is ready to merge.

list: **Must fix**: `apply` consumes a use on every call, even when the order already has that coupon. A double-click costs 2 uses, and repeated POSTs can use up a campaign. Check `order.couponCode` first, and add a same-order test.

**Question**: after a decline, a coupon makes checkout resend key `order-<id>` with a new amount, possibly 0. If the payment service rejects that, the order stays PENDING_PAYMENT and the user sees 500. Please confirm with the payment service docs.
**Suggestion**: an unparseable `expires_at` becomes Invalid Date, and the coupon never expires. Validate it, and state the time zone.
**Good**: check and increment in one UPDATE, a required `discountAmount` with DEFAULT 0, and tests on real SQLite that pin the charge amount.
Stated the purpose and a testable hypothesis (`max_uses` = customers) before reading code.
Carried a promise from unchanged code (checkout's double-click handling) into the review of new code.
Read a true comment and asked what it does not promise.
Pushed concrete values (two clicks, a typo'd date, a 0-yen charge) through code that looked right.
Checked a fix against the setup it relies on, and named what it still leaves open.
Separated what our code decides (plain Error leaves the order PENDING) from what the payment service decides.
Said "fine" only with a place in the repo to point at.
